question: According to the manual, what is a 'hazard'?
choice_a: Only a pedestrian crossing against a signal
choice_b: Any posted speed limit sign
choice_c: Only a vehicle that has already crashed
choice_d: Any road condition or other road user that is a possible danger
explanation: The manual defines a hazard as any road condition or other road user (driver, bicyclist, pedestrian) that is a possible danger.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.8.1 Importance of Seeing Hazards

question: Why does seeing hazards early let you be a more prepared driver?
choice_a: It removes the need to check your mirrors
choice_b: It allows you to increase your speed to get past it faster
choice_c: It lets you ignore the hazard completely
choice_d: You will have more time to act before a hazard becomes an emergency
explanation: Seeing hazards lets you be prepared: you will have more time to act if you see hazards before they become emergencies.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.8.1 Importance of Seeing Hazards

question: What is the difference between a hazard and an emergency, according to the manual's example of a car braking near a freeway exit?
choice_a: The car is a hazard until it actually cuts in front of you, at which point it becomes an emergency
choice_b: A hazard only exists on freeways, while an emergency can happen anywhere
choice_c: A hazard is more dangerous than an emergency
choice_d: There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable
explanation: In the manual's example, a car showing signs of uncertainty is a hazard; if that car actually cuts in front of you, it is no longer just a hazard, it is an emergency.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.8.1 Importance of Seeing Hazards

question: What are 'move-over laws' designed to address?
choice_a: The high number of law enforcement, EMS, fire, and roadside workers being struck while working at the roadside
choice_b: Speeding in school zones only
choice_c: Excessive noise from commercial vehicles
choice_d: Illegal parking in residential areas
explanation: Move-over laws were enacted because incidents of law enforcement, EMS, fire personnel, and roadside workers being struck while performing duties at the roadside are increasing.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.8.2 Hazardous Roads

question: When approaching an authorized emergency vehicle stopped on the roadside, what should you do if a lane change away from it is unsafe?
choice_a: Stop completely in your current lane
choice_b: Speed up to pass the vehicle quickly
choice_c: Change lanes anyway regardless of safety
choice_d: Slow down and proceed with caution while maintaining a safe speed for traffic conditions
explanation: If a lane change is unsafe, the manual instructs drivers to slow down and proceed with caution while maintaining a safe speed for traffic conditions.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.8.2 Hazardous Roads

question: Why are work zones considered a road hazard?
choice_a: Work zones never affect commercial vehicles
choice_b: They always have higher speed limits than normal
choice_c: They are only found on rural roads
choice_d: There may be narrower lanes, sharp turns, uneven surfaces, and distracted drivers
explanation: Work zones can have narrower lanes, sharp turns, or uneven surfaces, and other drivers are often distracted and drive unsafely near them.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.8.2 Hazardous Roads

question: What should you do near work zones to warn drivers behind you?
choice_a: Turn on your high beams
choice_b: Use your four-way flashers or brake lights
choice_c: Flash your headlights rapidly
choice_d: Sound your horn continuously
explanation: The manual advises using your four-way flashers or brake lights to warn drivers behind you near work zones.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.8.2 Hazardous Roads

question: Why can a drop off near the edge of the pavement be dangerous?
choice_a: It can tilt your vehicle toward the side of the road and make steering difficult
choice_b: It only affects motorcycles
choice_c: It has no effect on large vehicles
choice_d: It always causes a flat tire
explanation: A pavement drop off near the edge can tilt your vehicle toward the side of the road and make it hard to steer as you cross it.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.8.2 Hazardous Roads

question: Why should you be cautious of foreign objects, like cardboard boxes, in the road?
choice_a: They are always empty and harmless
choice_b: They can contain solid or heavy material and cause damage even though they appear harmless
choice_c: They improve traction when driven over
choice_d: They only affect bicycles
explanation: Obstacles that appear harmless, such as cardboard boxes, may actually contain solid or heavy material capable of causing damage.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.8.2 Hazardous Roads

question: Why are off ramps and on ramps that go downhill and turn at the same time especially dangerous?
choice_a: The downgrade makes it difficult to reduce speed while also turning
choice_b: They are only used by passenger cars
choice_c: They always have the highest posted speed limits
choice_d: There is never a need to slow down on them
explanation: Exits that go downhill and turn at the same time are especially dangerous because the downgrade makes it difficult to reduce speed, and braking and turning at the same time can be dangerous.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.8.2 Hazardous Roads

question: Why are vehicles with blocked vision, such as loaded station wagons or rental trucks, considered hazards?
choice_a: Their drivers may not be able to see others, or may not be used to their limited vision to the sides and rear
choice_b: They are exempt from traffic laws
choice_c: They are always driven faster than other vehicles
choice_d: They never need to change lanes
explanation: People who can't see others, such as drivers of vans, loaded station wagons, and rental trucks unfamiliar with their limited vision, are a dangerous hazard.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.8.3 Drivers Who Are Hazards

question: If you can only see the rear or front end of a vehicle at a blind intersection or alley, but not the driver, what should you assume?
choice_a: The driver can see you clearly
choice_b: The vehicle is parked and will not move
choice_c: The driver can't see you and may back out or enter your lane, so you should be prepared to stop
choice_d: You have the right of way in all cases
explanation: If you can only see the rear or front end of a vehicle but not the driver, the driver can't see you, so you should be alert and prepared to stop.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.8.3 Drivers Who Are Hazards

question: What clues suggest a parked vehicle may be about to move and become a hazard?
choice_a: A locked steering wheel
choice_b: Tinted windows
choice_c: A flat tire
choice_d: Movement inside the vehicle, brake lights, backup lights, or exhaust
explanation: Watch for movement inside a parked vehicle, or brake lights, backup lights, and exhaust as clues that a driver is about to move.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.8.3 Drivers Who Are Hazards

question: Why is a stopped bus considered a hazard?
choice_a: Passengers may cross in front of or behind the bus and often can't see you
choice_b: Buses never have working brake lights
choice_c: Buses are always parked illegally
choice_d: It is illegal to pass a stopped bus under any circumstance
explanation: Be careful of a stopped bus because passengers may cross in front of or behind it, and they often can't see approaching traffic.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.8.3 Drivers Who Are Hazards

question: What symbol warns you that a vehicle, such as farm machinery, is a slow-moving vehicle?
choice_a: A yellow diamond with a black exclamation point
choice_b: A green square with a white border
choice_c: A red triangle with an orange center
choice_d: A blue circle with a white arrow
explanation: Slow moving vehicles, such as mopeds, farm machinery, or tractors, may display the 'slow moving vehicle' symbol, a red triangle with an orange center.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.8.3 Drivers Who Are Hazards

question: Which of the following is listed as a clue that a driver may be impaired?
choice_a: Maintaining a constant, steady speed
choice_b: Weaving across the road or drifting from one side to another
choice_c: Coming to a complete stop at a stop sign
choice_d: Using a turn signal well before a turn
explanation: Weaving across the road or drifting from one side to another is listed as a clue of an impaired driver, along with leaving the road, stopping at the wrong time, and speeding up or slowing down suddenly.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.8.3 Drivers Who Are Hazards

question: Drivers making over-the-shoulder checks, especially motorcyclists and bicyclists, may be giving what kind of clue?
choice_a: That they are lost
choice_b: That their vehicle has mechanical problems
choice_c: That they are about to change lanes, even without a turn signal on
choice_d: That they intend to stop suddenly
explanation: Drivers making over-the-shoulder checks may be about to change lanes; these clues are most easily seen in motorcyclists and bicyclists.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.8.3 Drivers Who Are Hazards

question: What is a 'conflict' as described in the manual's discussion of hazards?
choice_a: A disagreement between two drivers after a crash
choice_b: A situation where you must change speed and/or direction to avoid hitting someone
choice_c: A mechanical failure in your vehicle
choice_d: A disagreement with a dispatcher
explanation: You are in conflict when you have to change speed and/or direction to avoid hitting someone; conflicts occur at intersections, merges, and lane changes.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.8.3 Drivers Who Are Hazards

question: Why are tourists unfamiliar with an area considered a hazard clue near freeway interchanges?
choice_a: They cannot legally drive commercial vehicles
choice_b: They may make unexpected actions like stopping in the middle of a block or changing lanes for no apparent reason
choice_c: They are required to use a special lane
choice_d: They always drive faster than posted limits
explanation: Confused or unfamiliar drivers, including tourists, may take unexpected actions such as stopping in the middle of a block, changing lanes without reason, or hesitating.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.8.3 Drivers Who Are Hazards

question: According to the manual, why should you always be looking for hazards and thinking about possible emergencies?
choice_a: It is only necessary in bad weather
choice_b: So you have time to plan a way out of any emergency that develops
choice_c: So you can drive faster with confidence
choice_d: So you can avoid using your mirrors
explanation: You look for hazards in order to have time to plan a way out of any emergency, making you a prepared, defensive driver.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.8.4 Always Have a Plan

question: How does the manual define a driver distraction?
choice_a: Only a mechanical failure in the vehicle
choice_b: Only the use of a cell phone
choice_c: Only conversations with passengers
choice_d: Anything that takes your attention away from driving
explanation: The manual defines a driver distraction as anything that takes your attention away from driving.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9 Distracted Driving

question: According to the Large Truck Crash Causation Study (LTCCS) cited in the manual, what percentage of large-truck crashes occurred when the CMV driver was externally distracted?
choice_a: 2 percent
choice_b: 39 percent
choice_c: 23 percent
choice_d: 8 percent
explanation: The LTCCS reported that 8 percent of large-truck crashes occurred when CMV drivers were externally distracted, and 2 percent occurred when internally distracted.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.1 The Distracted Driving Crash Problem

question: According to research cited in the manual, talking on a cell phone, even hands-free, saps the brain of what percentage of the energy it would ordinarily devote to safe driving?
explanation: Research indicates that talking on a cell phone, even hands-free, saps the brain of 39% of the energy it would ordinarily devote to safe driving.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.1 The Distracted Driving Crash Problem

question: What is one effect of distracted driving described in the manual?
choice_a: Improved reaction time
choice_b: Better vehicle handling
choice_c: Increased fuel efficiency
choice_d: Slowed perception, which may cause you to be delayed in perceiving or fail to perceive an important traffic event
explanation: Effects of distracted driving include slowed perception, which may delay or prevent perceiving an important traffic event, and delayed decision making.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.2 Effects of Distracted Driving

question: What is a 'physical distraction' as defined in the manual?
choice_a: One that causes you to take your hands off the wheel or eyes off the road, such as reaching for an object
choice_b: One that only involves emotional stress
choice_c: One that only occurs at night
choice_d: One caused solely by weather conditions
explanation: A physical distraction is one that causes you to take your hands off the wheel or eyes off the road, such as reaching for an object.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.3 Types of Distractions

question: What is a 'mental distraction' as defined in the manual?
choice_a: Activities that take your mind away from the road, such as engaging in conversation with a passenger
choice_b: Only distractions from other vehicles
choice_c: Only distractions caused by loud noises
choice_d: A distraction that always involves texting
explanation: A mental distraction is defined as activities that take your mind away from the road, such as conversation with a passenger or thinking about something else.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.3 Types of Distractions

question: Why does the manual describe talking on a cell phone or texting as an even greater risk than a purely physical or purely mental distraction?
choice_a: Because it only affects new drivers
choice_b: Because it is illegal in all vehicles, commercial or not
choice_c: Because it is both a physical and mental distraction at the same time
choice_d: Because it has no effect on reaction time
explanation: Activities like talking on a cell phone or sending/reading text messages involve both physical and mental distraction, creating an even greater chance a crash could happen.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.3 Types of Distractions

question: If you choose to use a mobile phone while operating a CMV under the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations, what type of phone use is permitted?
choice_a: Any phone use is completely prohibited with no exceptions
choice_b: Any hand-held device, as long as it is used briefly
choice_c: Only a hands-free mobile phone located close to you that can be operated to conduct a voice communication
choice_d: Texting only, never voice calls
explanation: If a driver chooses to use a mobile phone while operating a CMV, only a hands-free mobile phone located close to the driver that can be operated in compliance with the rule may be used.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.4 Cell/Mobile Phones

question: How many convictions of hand-held mobile telephone use while operating a CMV will result in CDL disqualification?
choice_a: Five convictions
choice_b: Convictions never result in disqualification for this offense
choice_c: One conviction
choice_d: Two or more convictions
explanation: A CDL will be disqualified after two or more convictions of any state law on hand-held mobile telephone use while operating a CMV.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.4 Cell/Mobile Phones

question: What is the CDL disqualification period for a second hand-held mobile phone offense within 3 years?
choice_a: 120 days
choice_b: 60 days
choice_c: 30 days
choice_d: 1 year
explanation: Disqualification is 60 days for the second hand-held mobile telephone offense within 3 years, and 120 days for three or more offenses within 3 years.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.4 Cell/Mobile Phones

question: Up to how much can a driver be civilly penalized for a hand-held mobile telephone violation while operating a CMV?
explanation: Each violation of the hand-held mobile telephone prohibition is subject to civil penalties on the driver in an amount up to $2,750; employers may face penalties up to $11,000.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.4 Cell/Mobile Phones

question: Up to how much can a motor carrier/employer be civilly penalized for allowing or requiring a driver to use a hand-held mobile telephone while driving?
explanation: Employers may be subject to civil penalties in an amount up to $11,000 for allowing or requiring drivers to use hand-held mobile telephones while driving.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.4 Cell/Mobile Phones

question: Is there an exception to the hand-held mobile telephone restriction for CMV drivers?
choice_a: Yes, but only for calls under 30 seconds
choice_b: Yes, an emergency exception allows use to communicate with law enforcement or other emergency services
choice_c: No exceptions exist under any circumstance
choice_d: Yes, but only when the vehicle is empty of cargo
explanation: There is an emergency exception that allows drivers to use hand-held mobile telephones if necessary to communicate with law enforcement officials or other emergency services.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.4 Cell/Mobile Phones

question: According to research cited in the manual, how many times greater are the odds of a safety-critical event for CMV drivers who dial a mobile telephone while driving compared to those who do not?
choice_a: 6 times greater
choice_b: 2 times greater
choice_c: 23.2 times greater
choice_d: 10 times greater
explanation: The odds of being involved in a safety-critical event are 6 times greater for CMV drivers who dial a mobile telephone while driving than for those who do not.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.4 Cell/Mobile Phones

question: On average, how many seconds did dialing drivers take their eyes off the forward roadway, according to the manual?
choice_a: 2.6 seconds
choice_b: 4.6 seconds
choice_c: 1.5 seconds
choice_d: 3.8 seconds
explanation: Dialing drivers took their eyes off the forward roadway for an average of 3.8 seconds, equating to 306 feet traveled at 55 mph -- about the length of a football field.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.4 Cell/Mobile Phones

question: Are hands-free cell phone devices less likely to cause distraction than hand-held devices, according to the manual?
choice_a: Hands-free devices are safer only in daylight
choice_b: No, hands-free devices are no less likely than hand-held phones to cause distraction because attention is diverted from the driving task either way
choice_c: Hands-free devices are only safe at low speeds
choice_d: Yes, hands-free devices eliminate all distraction
explanation: The manual notes that hands-free devices are no less likely than hand-held cell phones to cause distraction, since attention is diverted from the driving task while using either device.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.4 Cell/Mobile Phones

question: Why does the manual state that texting is even riskier than talking on a cell phone?
choice_a: Texting is not actually riskier than talking
choice_b: Texting is only possible while stopped
choice_c: Texting requires looking at a small screen and manipulating the keypad, involving both physical and mental distraction simultaneously
choice_d: Texting uses more battery power than calling
explanation: Texting is the most alarming distraction because it requires looking at a small screen and manipulating the keypad, involving both physical and mental distraction simultaneously.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.5 Texting

question: According to research cited in the manual, how many times greater are the odds of a safety-critical event for CMV drivers who text while driving compared to those who do not?
choice_a: 10 times greater
choice_b: 23.2 times greater
choice_c: 6 times greater
choice_d: 15 times greater
explanation: The odds of being involved in a safety-critical event are 23.2 times greater for CMV drivers who engage in texting while driving than for those who do not.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.5 Texting

question: On average, how many seconds does sending or receiving a text take a driver's eyes from the road, according to the manual?
choice_a: 2.1 seconds
choice_b: 3.8 seconds
choice_c: 4.6 seconds
choice_d: 6.0 seconds
explanation: Sending or receiving text takes a driver's eyes from the road for an average of 4.6 seconds, or 371 feet at 55 mph -- the length of an entire football field.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.5 Texting

question: How does the manual define 'texting' for purposes of the federal CMV driving prohibition?
choice_a: Only sending a text message via SMS
choice_b: Any use of a GPS navigation system
choice_c: Manually entering text into, or reading text from, an electronic device, including SMS, e-mail, instant messaging, or accessing a web page
choice_d: Only using a laptop computer while driving
explanation: Texting means manually entering text into, or reading text from, an electronic device, including short message service, e-mailing, instant messaging, or accessing a web page.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.5 Texting

question: What is the CDL disqualification period for a driver's second texting-while-driving offense within 3 years?
choice_a: 60 days
choice_b: 180 days
choice_c: 30 days
choice_d: 90 days
explanation: Disqualification is 60 days for a second texting offense within 3 years, and 120 days for three or more offenses within 3 years -- the same structure as the hand-held phone violation.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.5 Texting

question: Is there an emergency exception to the texting prohibition for CMV drivers?
choice_a: Yes, an emergency exception allows texting if necessary to communicate with law enforcement or other emergency services
choice_b: No exception exists
choice_c: Yes, but only to family members
choice_d: Yes, but only while the vehicle is off
explanation: There is an emergency exception that allows a driver to text if necessary to communicate with law enforcement officials or other emergency services.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.5 Texting

question: What happens to crash risk if drivers react a half-second slower because of distractions, according to the manual?
choice_a: Crashes decrease slightly
choice_b: There is no measurable effect
choice_c: Crashes triple only in bad weather
choice_d: Crashes double
explanation: The manual states that if drivers react a half-second slower because of distractions, crashes double.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.6 Don't Drive Distracted

question: What is one recommended step to eliminate in-vehicle distractions before driving begins?
choice_a: Keeping all communication devices turned on and ready
choice_b: Assessing all potential in-vehicle distractions before driving
choice_c: Waiting until an emergency occurs to make a plan
choice_d: Avoiding the use of mirrors
explanation: The manual recommends assessing all potential in-vehicle distractions before driving and developing a preventative plan to reduce or eliminate them.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.6 Don't Drive Distracted

question: Are drivers considered in compliance if they unsafely reach for a mobile phone but intend to use its hands-free function?
choice_a: Yes, intent to use hands-free always makes it compliant
choice_b: No, drivers are not in compliance if they unsafely reach for a mobile phone, even if they intend to use the hands-free feature
choice_c: Compliance only depends on vehicle speed
choice_d: Yes, as long as the phone is answered within one ring
explanation: Drivers are not in compliance if they unsafely reach for a mobile phone, even if they intend to use the hands-free function.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.6 Don't Drive Distracted

question: What should you do with your vehicle's mirrors and controls before you begin driving, according to the tips for avoiding distraction?
choice_a: Leave them as the previous driver set them
choice_b: Wait until you are on the highway to adjust them
choice_c: Only adjust mirrors, never other controls
choice_d: Adjust all vehicle controls and mirrors to your preference before driving
explanation: One tip to avoid becoming distracted is to adjust all vehicle controls and mirrors to your preference before driving begins.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.6 Don't Drive Distracted
